basis: New mission, no workbook source; authored per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Sensitive topic (student mental health / suicide prevention): informative, supportive framing used throughout; the mortality statistic is stated once, respectfully, without graphic detail, and every slide from Part 3 onward points toward concrete help; the talk closes on the 1925 hotline number and an encouraging, agency-focused message. Facts and sources: 23.1% of university students showed depressive-emotion tendencies in a 2024 survey (June-Oct 2024, n=3,264) by the Counseling Psychologists Association, R.O.C. (中華民國諮商心理師公會全國聯合會); academic pressure and financial difficulty were the top-cited stress sources, future-planning pressure ranked highest across all year levels, third-year students reported the highest overall stress (Heho健康 2024 coverage; epochtimes.com 2024-12-22 report of the same survey). One university (National Chung Cheng University) staff-reported rise from ~6% to ~8-9% with clear depressive symptoms over a decade, used as one illustrative, attributed data point, not a national figure (ccu.edu.tw news page). MOHW mortality data: self-harm is the #2 leading cause of death among Taiwanese aged 15-24 (~25%), and the #1 cause of death for young women in that age band (~34.4%), as reported via the same ccu.edu.tw article citing MOHW statistics -- stated once, respectfully, no method/graphic detail. Student Guidance Law (學生輔導法) revised to move the required university student-to-professional-counselor ratio from 1:1200 to 1:900; MOE began adjusting subsidy budgets from Jan 2024; ~216 additional counseling positions estimated needed nationwide (udn.com 2024 and 2025 coverage). Retention problem: campus counselor positions often pay only ~NT$44,000/month on one-year contracts, making them hard to fill even when funded (twreporter.org, "大專心理師耗竭前的SOS"). Access gap: ~78.5% of students who might benefit do not use their campus counseling center, citing lack of time, distance, and privacy concerns (Heho健康, "大學生心理諮商需求高"). Psychological leave (心理假) exists at many Taiwanese universities but only ~7.5% of students have ever used it (epochtimes.com 2024 report, and ccu.edu.tw). 1925 hotline (依舊愛我): MOHW-run, free, 24/7, single number since Dec 2019 (previously 0800-788-995); documented call volume grew from 27,926 calls (2005) to 78,108 calls (2018, ~6,500/month), reaching ~8,000 calls/month by 2019 -- described in the script only as "has grown steadily for years," not with an unverified recent-year total (mohw.gov.tw hotline history pages). Stigma/help-seeking context: a national adolescent survey (兒福聯盟) found ~39% of youth who struggle emotionally tell no one, correlated with perceived stigma -- used as general context for why stigma, not only access, is part of the problem (udn.com 2024 coverage of 兒福聯盟 survey). No specific 2023-2025 hotline call total was found and confirmed, so none is stated as a precise figure. Register and structure per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md; calibration matched to content/authored/levels/sdg13-1.*.json.

slides.1: A quarter of the people sitting in a room like this one, statistically speaking, are carrying more psychological strain than their expression ever reveals. That figure is not intuition, but the result of actual measurement.
slides.2: SDG 3 establishes a single global objective, and mental wellbeing sits inside that objective exactly as firmly as physical health does. Taiwan has enshrined that principle in law, though whether daily practice matches the promise is another matter entirely.
slides.3: From outside, a university schedule reads as nothing but classes, clubs and friends. What that timetable hides is the weight a considerable number of students are quietly carrying underneath it.
slides.4: According to a 2024 national survey, 23.1 percent of university students showed signs of depression, and that figure has been rising steadily for roughly ten years. Heavy coursework and money strain were named most often as the top causes.
slides.5: Coursework and money dominate whenever students are actually asked about the source of their pressure. Those in their third year carry the single heaviest load of anyone, arriving precisely when an entire future must also be planned.
slides.6: This next figure is difficult, but leaving it unsaid would be worse. Among Taiwanese aged 15 to 24, self-harm has become the second most common cause of death, and everything else in this talk follows from that single, sobering fact.
slides.7: Legislation has finally caught up with demand in this area. The required counselor-to-student ratio at universities has moved from one in 1,200 to one in 900, a transition that should put genuine, trained support within significantly easier reach.
slides.8: If you remember only one single number from this entire talk, make it 1925. Since its establishment, this free, round-the-clock hotline has grown substantially busier with each passing year, and someone consistently, reliably answers it, day or night.
slides.9: A formal policy called psychological leave already sits in most university handbooks, letting any struggling student step back without shame. What remains unclear is whether students actually use that right, a question the next few slides take up directly.
slides.10: Hiring more staff sounds like a simple fix on paper. Converting that instruction into an actual, funded position is another matter entirely, and schools without adequate budget will struggle to keep those positions staffed for long.
slides.11: A single, fixed office hour is an oddly restrictive gate for something this time-sensitive. Evening slots, an online chat option or a confidential drop-in space would each widen that gate considerably, and a wider gate saves lives.
slides.12: Instead of merely reacting once a crisis has already occurred, universities can intervene earlier. Courses can teach students to recognise stress in themselves and in their friends, well before it escalates into something harder to manage.
slides.13: Funding a position and filling it are two different things entirely. Low pay on a one-year contract makes these new counselor roles a hard sell, and an unfilled seat keeps the better ratio just a number on paper.
slides.14: Simply adding counselors does not resolve the underlying problem. Many students capable of benefiting nonetheless avoid the office, even with help located down the corridor. It is privacy that concerns them most, followed closely by time and distance.
slides.15: Only a small fraction of students, roughly 7.5 percent by one estimate, ever actually use the psychological leave written into university policy. Possessing that right on paper does not translate into feeling safe enough to exercise it.
slides.16: Two distinct gaps operate here simultaneously, not one. Capacity concerns whether enough trained staff exist at all, while comfort concerns whether students feel safe enough to approach them, and addressing only one leaves the other exactly as wide as before.
slides.17: Taken together, the picture is genuinely encouraging: a stronger law, a working hotline, and leave policies written on the books. It is stigma that continues to drag this progress backward, quietly, far more than any remaining staffing gap.
slides.18: This talk is not asking you to repair the entire system by tomorrow. A friend who suddenly seems different, met with one sincere, well-timed question, already represents meaningful action, sometimes even a life-changing one.
slides.19: Warning signs rarely announce themselves loudly: reduced sleep, fading energy, a quiet, gradual drift away from friends. Recognising them is only half of it, though, since knowing which number to say immediately afterward, 1925, can genuinely change what happens next.
slides.20: Weakness is not the right word for reaching out, since what it actually takes is courage, the courage to admit that something is genuinely difficult right now. Support is there, entirely free of charge, one phone call away: 1925.
